shortDescription: Chipotle NYSE:CMG shares have moved significantly higher in recent days, boosted by reports that Starbucks NASDAQ:SBUX was readying a bid for the fast casual restaurant chain.But could other bidders emerge for the popular burrito vendor?Seeking Alpha analysts APAC Research and Daniel Jones weigh in…

children: Chipotle
shares have moved significantly higher in recent days, boosted by reports that Starbucks
was readying a bid for the fast casual restaurant chain.
But could other bidders emerge for the popular burrito vendor?
Seeking Alpha analysts
and
weigh in.

: To be honest, I’m unconvinced that a Starbucks/Chipotle merger would benefit either company, and for investors, the tie-up would make it more difficult to evaluate the separate businesses. That said, with Starbucks Brian Niccol having previously led Chipotle
, synergy may be of secondary importance, with familiarity taking the lead.
Still, I believe CMG will remain independent for now. If it is acquired, I’d expect a private equity firm like LongRange Capital (which bought Pizza Hut recently) to emerge as the winning bidder.
Daniel Jones: Things have been rather interesting for shareholders of Chipotle Mexican Grill
as of late. Rumors have been circulating that the company could be bought out, with prices ranging between $40 and $45 per share.

As of market close on Wednesday, the stock was at $30.77, which would indicate some meaningful upside for shareholders. And yet, that actually represents a drop compared to when I reaffirmed the business as a Hold candidate back in September. The firm had experienced strong revenue growth and positive comparable sales, but margin pressures caused by inflation and rising costs proved problematic.

In some respects, a buyout from some other party might represent a good exit for investors. But I think it is unlikely that it will get an offer from another publicly traded player in the restaurant industry.
The first company that does pop into mind when I hear about a possible buyout is McDonald’s

. Up until Chipotle's IPO in January 2006 and a subsequent divestiture of its remaining shares in October of that year, McDonald’s owned most of the business. Selling it was one of the worst things McDonald’s has ever done. The buyout price translated to a market capitalization of around $716M. But today, Chipotle
is the third largest restaurant operator on the market, with a market capitalization of $39B.
During that same window of time, McDonald’s
has gone from a market cap of $44B to $163B. In essence, Chipotle
has been catching up to its prior owner. Furthermore, McDonald’s certainly has the financial capability to make a transaction like this happen.
Other players in the restaurant space make sense conceptually, but a deal might be difficult. The second largest player is Starbucks

, with a market cap of $107B. In previous years, it would have been a great candidate to buy out Chipotle. But it has been dealing with its own restructuring activities and recently transitioned its Chinese operations into a licensed model. I don’t see it going out on a limb to make such a large purchase right now. Not everyone agrees with me, though. Semafor said Starbucks
could be an ideal partner, in part because its current CEO, Brian Niccol, used to run Chipotle
The fourth largest player out there is Yum! Brands
, which owns famous names such as KFC and Taco Bell. But it has simplified in recent years, selling off Pizza Hut in a deal worth $2.7B. Restaurant Brands International
, which owns Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes, and Firehouse Subs, is another candidate.
Then there is Darden Restaurants

, which owns Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse. Operationally speaking, it might actually be the best publicly traded company to make a transaction happen because, unlike the others, its emphasis is on casual and fine dining, as opposed to fast food. Admittedly, Chipotle

is a fast casual restaurant, which puts it somewhere between fast food and casual dining. But it is also known as a quality operator that gets customers to shell out a little extra cash compared to a traditional fast food joint.
However, with a market capitalization of only $23B and net debt of $2.4B, Darden
would either need to take on a tremendous amount of leverage, issue so many shares that it would be essentially equivalent to Chipotle
absorbing it, or a combination of the two. And any sort of transaction that involves a lot of debt would further pressure Chipotle's margins.

I think it is more likely that a private equity firm or some other private buyer will purchase Chipotle Mexican Grill if a deal does occur. This would not be unprecedented. European investment group JAB Holding Company purchased Panera Bread in 2017 for $7.5B. And in 2021, it rolled Caribou Coffee and Einstein Bros. Bagels into Panera's corporate structure.
It's certainly not unthinkable that some other big firm might take Chipotle
off the market entirely. But I do think it is more likely that the company will remain publicly traded.
(Daniel Jones runs the SA investment newsletter Crude Value Insights.)
